lead: Sources push energy into a circuit. An independent source fixes its own voltage or current, whatever the rest of the circuit does. A dependent (controlled) source sets its voltage or current as a fixed multiple of a voltage or current somewhere else in the circuit; it is how transistors and op-amps appear in circuit equations. Real batteries and supplies are neither perfect, so each ideal source also has a practical model with an internal resistance.
prereq: You need: the passive sign convention and power p = vi from Circuit elements R, L, C.

blocks.text: An ideal voltage source keeps its terminal voltage at Vs volts for any current; the external circuit decides the current. Its symbol is a circle with + and − marks (a circle with a ∼ for a sinusoidal source). On a graph of terminal voltage v against current i its characteristic is a horizontal line v = Vs, so its internal resistance is zero.

An ideal current source keeps its current at Is amperes for any terminal voltage; the external circuit decides the voltage. Its symbol is a circle with an arrow showing the direction of the current. On the same graph its characteristic is a vertical line i = Is, so its internal resistance is infinite.

items: Never short-circuit an ideal voltage source: i = V<sub>s</sub>/0 has no finite value. Never open-circuit an ideal current source: the voltage needed to push I<sub>s</sub> through a break has no finite value.
Two ideal voltage sources of different values cannot sit in parallel (KVL fails), and two ideal current sources of different values cannot sit in series (KCL fails).
A voltage source set to zero is a short circuit; a current source set to zero is an open circuit. The network theorems use this when they switch independent sources off.

blocks.text: A real battery loses part of its EMF inside itself. Model it as an ideal Vs in series with an internal resistance Rs. KVL round the source gives the terminal voltage v = Vs − iRs: it equals Vs on open circuit (i = 0) and falls linearly as the load current rises, reaching zero at the short-circuit current isc = Vs/Rs. A good voltage source has Rs much smaller than the load.

A practical current source is an ideal Is in parallel with a resistance Rp. KCL at its terminal gives i = Is − v/Rp: part of Is leaks through Rp, more as the terminal voltage rises. A good current source has Rp much larger than the load. When Is = Vs/Rs and Rp = Rs the two models give the same terminal line; that is source transformation.

A dependent source has a control (a voltage vx or a current ix measured elsewhere) and an output that behaves as a voltage source or a current source. Its symbol is a diamond, with + and − for a voltage output or an arrow for a current output, and the control expression written beside it.

A dependent source is an active element: it can deliver more power than its control receives, which is what amplification means. When you write circuit equations, keep the control variable as an unknown and add one extra equation that ties it to the other unknowns. Unlike an independent source, a dependent source is never switched off on its own; the network theorems keep it in the circuit.

examples.question: A 2 V source drives a 1 kΩ resistor; the voltage across this resistor is v<sub>x</sub>. A VCCS of gain g = 2 mS, controlled by v<sub>x</sub>, pushes its current into a 2.5 kΩ load. Find the output voltage, the voltage gain, the power the VCCS delivers and the power the 2 V source delivers.
steps: Input side: the 1 kΩ resistor sits directly across the 2 V source, so v<sub>x</sub> = 2 V and the input current is 2 V / 1000 Ω = 2 mA.
VCCS output: i = g v<sub>x</sub> = 2 × 10⁻³ S × 2 V = 4 × 10⁻³ A = 4 mA.
This current flows through the 2.5 kΩ load: v<sub>out</sub> = 4 × 10⁻³ A × 2500 Ω = 10 V.

Power delivered by the VCCS = 10 V × 4 mA = 40 mW. Power delivered by the 2 V source = 2 V × 2 mA = 4 mW. The dependent source delivers ten times the input power: it is active, and the extra energy comes from the supply that powers the real amplifier.
examples.answer: v<sub>out</sub> = 10 V, gain 5; the VCCS delivers 40 mW while the input source delivers only 4 mW.

examples.question: A 12 V battery has an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω. Find the terminal voltage, the load power and the power lost inside for loads of 11.5 Ω, 5.5 Ω and 1.5 Ω, and the short-circuit current.
steps: Model: 12 V in series with 0.5 Ω, so i = 12/(R<sub>L</sub> + 0.5) and v = 12 − 0.5i.
5.5 Ω: i = 12/6 = 2 A; v = 12 − 1 = 11 V; load power 11 × 2 = 22 W; inside loss 2² × 0.5 = 2 W.
1.5 Ω: i = 12/2 = 6 A; v = 12 − 3 = 9 V; load power 9 × 6 = 54 W; inside loss 6² × 0.5 = 18 W. Check: 54 + 18 = 72 W = 12 V × 6 A.
Short circuit (R<sub>L</sub> = 0): i<sub>sc</sub> = 12/0.5 = 24 A, v = 0, and all 288 W is lost inside the battery.
examples.answer: Terminal voltages 11.5 V, 11 V and 9 V; load powers 11.5 W, 22 W and 54 W; internal losses 0.5 W, 2 W and 18 W; short-circuit current 24 A.

traps: Treating a dependent source as independent: its value changes whenever its control changes, so keep the control as an unknown.
Dropping the gain unit: μ and β are pure numbers, g is in siemens and r in ohms. Convert 2 mS to 0.002 S before multiplying.
Drawing a dependent source as a circle. The diamond marks a dependent source; the circle is for an independent one.
Switching a source off the wrong way: a dead voltage source becomes a short circuit, a dead current source becomes an open circuit.
Quoting the EMF as the terminal voltage of a loaded practical source. Under load v = V<sub>s</sub> − iR<sub>s</sub>, which is less than V<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: Name the four dependent sources and give the unit of the gain of each.
quiz.a: VCVS (μ, no unit), VCCS (g, siemens), CCVS (r, ohms), CCCS (β, no unit).

quiz.q: Why does an ideal voltage source not fix its current?
quiz.a: It fixes only its terminal voltage. KVL and the elements connected to it decide how much current flows, so the current can take any value.

quiz.q: Why must an ideal current source never be left open-circuited?
quiz.a: It forces I<sub>s</sub> through its terminals. With an open circuit there is no path, so KCL cannot be met with a finite voltage; the model breaks down.

quiz.q: A VCVS has μ = 4 and v<sub>x</sub> = 2.5 V. A CCCS has β = 50 and i<sub>x</sub> = 12 mA. Find both outputs.
quiz.a: VCVS: v = μv<sub>x</sub> = 4 × 2.5 = 10 V. CCCS: i = βi<sub>x</sub> = 50 × 12 mA = 600 mA = 0.6 A.

quiz.q: A practical voltage source has V<sub>s</sub> = 12 V and R<sub>s</sub> = 2 Ω. The load draws 1.5 A. Find the terminal voltage.
quiz.a: v = V<sub>s</sub> − iR<sub>s</sub> = 12 − 1.5 × 2 = 9 V; an ideal source would hold 12 V.

quiz.q: A student writes: g = 3 S and v<sub>x</sub> = 2 V, so i = 6 mA. Find the mistake and the correct current.
quiz.a: Siemens times volts gives amperes, not milliamperes: i = g v<sub>x</sub> = 3 S × 2 V = 6 A (6000 mA). The student attached the wrong prefix.

quiz.q: A source reads 9 V on open circuit and 8 V when it supplies 0.5 A. Find its practical model and its short-circuit current.
quiz.a: Open circuit gives V<sub>s</sub> = 9 V. Under load 8 = 9 − 0.5R<sub>s</sub>, so R<sub>s</sub> = 2 Ω. Short-circuit current = 9/2 = 4.5 A. Model: 9 V in series with 2 Ω (or 4.5 A in parallel with 2 Ω).

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators name the four dependent sources E (VCVS), G (VCCS), H (CCVS) and F (CCCS), so these letters are worth searching in any SPICE manual. Transistor datasheets give the transconductance g<sub>m</sub> of a VCCS model, and op-amp datasheets give the open-loop gain that plays the part of μ. Battery datasheets quote internal resistance so that the practical model above can predict sag under load. Search next for small-signal models and controlled sources in SPICE.
